title: What happens when you open a website
intro: When you type a website address into your browser and press Enter, a surprisingly long chain of events happens in a fraction of a second. In this lesson, you will follow that journey from the URL you typed to the finished page you see on your screen.
body:
## The journey starts with a URL A **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a resource on the web. You use URLs every day, even if you do not normally think about their individual parts. ~~~widget request-journey ~~~ For example: ~~~text https://example.com/products/shoes?size=42&colour=black ~~~ A URL can contain several pieces of information: - `https` is the **protocol**. It tells the browser which communication rules to use. - `example.com` is the **hostname**. It identifies the website's server address by name. - `/products/shoes` is the **path**. It identifies the resource or location you want. - `?size=42&colour=black` is the **query string**. It contains additional parameters sent with the request. - A URL can also contain a **fragment**, such as `#reviews`, which usually tells the browser to move to a particular part of the current document. You do not need to remember every part immediately. The important idea is that a URL gives the browser enough information to figure out what you are asking for and how to communicate with the server. ## Step 1: Finding the server with DNS Computers communicate using **IP addresses**, such as `203.0.113.10`. People generally prefer names such as `example.com` because they are easier to remember. This is where **DNS** (Domain Name System) comes in. DNS is essentially the naming system that helps translate a hostname into an IP address. When you visit a website, your browser may need to ask a DNS server something like: > "What IP address belongs to example.com?" The DNS system finds the appropriate answer and returns an IP address. The browser can then use that address to contact the server. DNS is not necessarily contacted every time you open a website. Your computer, browser, operating system, network, or DNS provider may already have the answer stored in a **cache**. A cache is temporary stored information that can be reused instead of retrieving it again. This is one of the first places where caching can make the web faster. ## Step 2: Connecting to the server Now the browser knows where the server is. It needs to establish a connection. For a typical modern HTTPS website, this involves **TCP** and **TLS**. **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) is a communication protocol that helps two computers establish a reliable connection and exchange data in the correct order. You can think of it as creating a dependable communication channel between the browser and the server. Then there is **TLS** (Transport Layer Security). TLS encrypts the communication between your browser and the server so that other people on the network cannot simply read the information being exchanged. This is why you see `https://` rather than just `http://` on most modern websites. HTTPS is HTTP communication protected by TLS. The exact technical process behind TCP and TLS is more complicated than this, but you do not need to understand every packet to build web applications. A useful mental model is: ~~~text DNS → find the server TCP → establish reliable communication TLS → protect the communication HTTP → exchange web data ~~~ ## Step 3: Sending an HTTP request Once the connection is ready, the browser can send an **HTTP request** to the server. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules used for exchanging requests and responses on the web. A simplified request might look like this: ~~~http GET /products/shoes?size=42 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Accept: text/html ~~~ `GET` is an HTTP method. It tells the server that the client wants to retrieve something. The path tells the server which resource was requested. Headers provide additional information about the request. The **client** is the program making the request. In this example, the browser is the client. The **server** receives the request and decides what to do with it. ## Step 4: The backend does its work This is where the **backend** can enter the journey. The backend is the part of an application that runs on a server. It can contain business logic, authentication, validation, database access, and other operations that should not happen directly in the user's browser. Imagine you open an online shop's product page. The browser might request: ~~~text GET /products/123 ~~~ The backend could receive that request, find product `123` in a database, check whether the product is available, and create a response. In this course, we will use **Spring Boot** for the backend and **PostgreSQL** for the database. The backend might therefore have a journey of its own: ~~~text Browser ↓ Spring Boot ↓ PostgreSQL ↓ Spring Boot ↓ Browser ~~~ The browser does not normally communicate directly with PostgreSQL. The backend provides a controlled layer between the browser and the database. ## Step 5: Receiving the HTTP response The server sends an **HTTP response** back to the browser. A simplified response could look like this: ~~~http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html ... ~~~ The first line contains a **status code**. `200 OK` means the request was successfully handled. The response also contains headers. For example, `Content-Type` tells the browser what kind of content it received. The response body contains the actual data. For a traditional website, this could be HTML. Other requests might return CSS, JavaScript, images, JSON data, or other resources. ## Step 6: The browser processes HTML Receiving HTML is not the end of the journey. The browser has to turn the files it receives into the page you can interact with. ~~~diagram {"type": "flow", "title": "From bytes to pixels", "caption": "HTML and CSS are parsed into two trees, combined, laid out and painted. JavaScript can change both trees at any time.", "nodes": [{"id": "html", "label": "HTML", "kind": "file"}, {"id": "js", "label": "JavaScript", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "css", "label": "CSS", "kind": "file"}, {"id": "dom", "label": "DOM", "sub": "element tree", "highlight": true}, {"id": "cssom", "label": "CSSOM", "sub": "style rules"}, {"id": "rt", "label": "Render tree", "sub": "visible elements + styles"}, {"id": "layout", "label": "Layout", "sub": "sizes and positions"}, {"id": "paint", "label": "Paint", "sub": "pixels on screen", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "html", "to": "dom", "label": "parse"}, {"from": "css", "to": "cssom", "label": "parse"}, {"from": "dom", "to": "rt"}, {"from": "cssom", "to": "rt"}, {"from": "rt", "to": "layout"}, {"from": "layout", "to": "paint"}, {"from": "js", "to": "dom", "label": "changes", "dashed": true}]} ~~~ HTML describes the structure and meaning of the document. For example: ~~~html

Products

Welcome to our shop.

~~~ The browser parses this HTML and builds an in-memory structure called the **DOM** (Document Object Model). The DOM represents the elements of the page as a tree-like structure. You can imagine it like this: ~~~text Document ├── h1 │ └── "Products" └── p └── "Welcome to our shop." ~~~ JavaScript can interact with this structure. This is one reason the DOM is so important for frontend development. ## CSS changes how the page looks HTML provides structure, but **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) describes presentation and layout. For example: ~~~css h1 { font-size: 32px; } ~~~ The browser downloads and processes CSS files, determines which rules apply to which HTML elements, and calculates how those elements should be displayed. The browser then performs the work required to display the page. This overall process is commonly called **rendering**. Rendering includes determining the layout of elements and eventually drawing the visible result on the screen. You do not need to memorize the browser's internal rendering pipeline yet. The important idea is that HTML gives the browser structure, CSS gives it presentation rules, and the browser combines that information to produce the visual page. ## JavaScript makes the page interactive JavaScript can add behaviour to the page. For example, JavaScript could respond when you click a button, validate a form, update part of the page, or request additional information from a backend. A modern application might work like this: ~~~text HTML → page structure CSS → appearance and layout JavaScript → behaviour and interaction Backend → server-side logic and data Database → persistent application data ~~~ This separation is not absolute. Modern frameworks can blur some of these boundaries, but it is an excellent mental model for starting your full-stack journey. ## Where React fits In this course, we will use **React** for the frontend. React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Instead of manually changing every part of a page yourself, you describe UI components and how they should appear based on application state and data. For example, a React application might request product information from a Spring Boot backend. Spring Boot might retrieve the information from PostgreSQL and return it as JSON. The flow could look like: ~~~text React in the browser ↓ HTTP request ↓ Spring Boot backend ↓ PostgreSQL database ↓ Spring Boot response ↓ React updates the interface ~~~ We will build this kind of communication step by step later in the course. ## Why some files come from cache You may notice that a website sometimes loads much faster the second time you visit it. One reason is **caching**. ~~~callout tip See the cache at work Open DevTools → **Network**, reload the page, and look at the *Size* column: files served “(memory cache)” or “(disk cache)” never left your computer. Tick **Disable cache** while developing so you always see your latest CSS and JavaScript. ~~~ A cache stores previously retrieved information so it can potentially be reused. For example, suppose a website uses the same logo image on many pages. Downloading that image every time would waste time and bandwidth. The browser can store a copy locally and reuse it when appropriate. The browser can cache many kinds of resources, including CSS files, JavaScript files, images, and other responses. Caching is controlled by HTTP response headers and other browser rules. A server can tell the browser how long certain resources may be considered fresh. This also explains something you will eventually encounter as a developer: you change a CSS or JavaScript file, but the browser appears to show the old version. Sometimes the code really is old because a cached resource is being reused. Developer tools give you ways to inspect and control caching while developing. ## Frontend and backend in the complete journey It is useful to separate two major areas of a web application. The **frontend** is the part that runs in the user's browser. In our course, React will be the main frontend technology. It handles the user interface and interactions. The **backend** runs on a server. Spring Boot will handle server-side application logic and provide APIs that the frontend can call. The database stores persistent information. PostgreSQL will be our database technology. A simplified complete journey looks like this: ~~~text You enter a URL ↓ Browser checks cached information ↓ DNS finds the server's IP address ↓ Browser establishes a secure connection ↓ Browser sends an HTTP request ↓ Spring Boot receives the request ↓ Spring Boot may query PostgreSQL ↓ Spring Boot sends an HTTP response ↓ Browser receives HTML/CSS/JS or application data ↓ Browser builds the DOM and calculates the layout ↓ Browser renders the page ↓ JavaScript makes it interactive ~~~ Not every request follows exactly this sequence. For example, a React application may initially download JavaScript and then make additional HTTP requests for application data. Browsers also reuse existing connections and cached resources whenever possible. Still, this model gives you a strong foundation for understanding what happens underneath a website. ## The whole trip in a few steps When you open a website, start thinking of it as a journey rather than a single action. 1. **The URL tells the browser what you want and how to communicate.** 2. **DNS helps turn the hostname into an IP address.** 3. **TCP and TLS establish a reliable and secure connection.** 4. **HTTP carries requests from the browser to the server and responses back.** 5. **The backend can process requests and communicate with the database.** 6. **The browser processes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, builds the DOM, calculates layout, and renders the result.** 7. **Caches let the browser reuse resources instead of downloading everything again.** Once you understand this journey, technologies such as React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL stop looking like isolated tools. You can start seeing where each one belongs in the bigger picture of a web application.
takeaways: A URL contains information such as the protocol, hostname, path, and query parameters.
DNS helps the browser find the server associated with a hostname.
HTTP is used to exchange requests and responses, while HTTPS protects that communication with TLS.
The browser turns HTML into a DOM, applies CSS, runs JavaScript, and renders the resulting interface.
React runs mainly in the frontend, Spring Boot handles backend logic, and PostgreSQL stores persistent data.

quiz.question: What is the main job of DNS when you open a website?
options: It translates a hostname into an IP address.
It converts HTML into CSS.
It stores the website's database.
It encrypts every image on the page.
quiz.explanation: DNS helps map human-friendly hostnames such as example.com to IP addresses that computers can use to communicate.

quiz.question: What does TLS provide when you use HTTPS?
options: A database for the website.
Encryption and protection for the communication.
The HTML structure of the page.
The JavaScript framework used by the site.
quiz.explanation: TLS protects data exchanged between the browser and server by encrypting the communication.

quiz.question: What is the DOM?
options: A type of database server.
A DNS configuration file.
An in-memory representation of a document's structure.
A protocol used to encrypt HTTP.
quiz.explanation: The browser parses HTML and creates the DOM, which represents the document's elements in a structure that scripts can work with.

quiz.question: Which part of our course stack is responsible for server-side application logic?
options: PostgreSQL
CSS
React
Spring Boot
quiz.explanation: Spring Boot will be used for the backend, where server-side application logic and API endpoints can run.

quiz.question: Why can a browser load a previously visited resource without downloading it again?
options: The browser may have a cached copy.
DNS permanently stores the entire website.
TCP automatically creates a new HTML page.
The database is copied into the browser every time.
quiz.explanation: Browsers can cache resources such as images, CSS, and JavaScript so they can be reused when appropriate.

exercise.title: Build a URL parser
exercise.task: Create a function named `parseUrl(address)` that uses the browser's built-in `URL` class to parse a URL. It must return an object with the exact properties `protocol`, `host`, `path`, and `query`; `protocol` must not contain the trailing colon, `host` must contain only the hostname without a port, and `path` must contain the pathname. Convert the URL's search parameters into a plain object stored in `query`, using parameter names as keys and their values as strings. The tests expect the function to be available as a top-level function named `parseUrl`.
exercise.hint: The `URL` object provides `protocol`, `hostname`, and `pathname` directly. For the query parameters, `url.searchParams.entries()` gives key-value pairs that can be converted into a plain object with `Object.fromEntries()`.

tests.name: It parses a simple URL
tests.code:
const result = parseUrl('https://example.com/products/shoes');
return result.protocol === 'https' && result.host === 'example.com' && result.path === '/products/shoes' && Object.keys(result.query).length === 0;

tests.name: It removes the port from the host
tests.code:
const result = parseUrl('http://localhost:8080/api/products');
return result.protocol === 'http' && result.host === 'localhost' && result.path === '/api/products';

tests.name: It parses query parameters
tests.code:
const result = parseUrl('https://example.com/search?q=shoes&page=2');
return result.query.q === 'shoes' && result.query.page === '2' && Object.keys(result.query).length === 2;

tests.name: It handles encoded query values
tests.code:
const result = parseUrl('https://example.com/search?q=red%20shoes&sort=price');
return result.query.q === 'red shoes' && result.query.sort === 'price';

tests.name: It keeps the pathname separate from the query
